subtitle: Supervisors have an important role when an employee asks for a reasonable accommodation. You will learn to respond promptly, protect the employee’s privacy and help an effective adjustment work in daily practice.
scope: For DHS supervisors and managers who receive employment accommodation requests or help implement approved adjustments. The course teaches the supervisor’s contribution, not medical assessment or unilateral accommodation decisions. Follow current agency procedures and involve the agency ADA Coordinator for formal questions.
introTranscript: An accommodation conversation often starts in ordinary words: a person explains that a medical condition makes part of their work difficult and asks for a change. A supervisor’s first response can make the process clear and respectful, or leave the person unsure whether help is available. This course follows practice examples involving an applicant and employees. You will recognize requests, discuss the work without asking for medical records, route questions to the proper decision maker, protect confidentiality, implement approved changes and follow up. The aim is equal opportunity and effective work, with responsibility shared clearly rather than left to the employee alone.

lessons.title: Recognize the request in ordinary words
lessons.summary: A request does not need a diagnosis, a special phrase or a completed form before a supervisor responds.
lessons.objective: Recognize a possible accommodation request when a person links a needed change to a medical condition.
objectives: Recognize a possible accommodation request when a person links a needed change to a medical condition.
Give a clear first response without promising an outcome outside your authority.
Identify the next step for an applicant’s request before an interview.
takeaways: A request can be spoken, written or electronic.
Acknowledge the request and promptly connect it to the appropriate decision maker.
Do not wait for special words or decide that a person is ineligible because their disability is not visible.
lessons.statement: The first response should make the next step easier to understand, not make the person prove they know the right vocabulary.

image.caption: A respectful response begins with the person’s request and the work they need to do.

intro.heading: Listen for a barrier and a requested change
intro.body:
A practice DSD analyst tells a supervisor, “Because of a medical condition, the long video meetings are difficult. Could we discuss a different way for me to take part?” This may be an accommodation request even though the analyst has not said ADA or reasonable accommodation. MMB Policy 1433 allows requests in ordinary spoken, written or electronic communication. The process begins as soon as possible when the request is made; a later written record supports processing but is not a reason to ignore the first conversation.

A useful first response acknowledges what you heard, explains that you will connect the request with the appropriate decision maker and tells the person what happens next. You can ask about the task they need to perform and the adjustment they want considered. Do not ask for medical records or demand proof yourself. The agency ADA Coordinator manages appropriate medical documentation, and the formal process determines whether and how an accommodation is provided.

Requests can also come from applicants. An interview accommodation concerns an equal opportunity to compete, rather than an assumption about whether the applicant can do the job. Promptly route the request and coordinate the interview arrangements through the appropriate staff. Keep disability-related questions out of ordinary pre-offer selection discussions.

If someone describes difficulty but does not mention a medical connection, do not diagnose them or insist that they have a disability. You can discuss the work barrier and explain the available support route. When you are unsure how to respond, seek the ADA Coordinator’s guidance. A prompt, respectful response does not require you to resolve every legal question on the spot.

inThisLesson: Identify a request without special vocabulary.
Practice a calm first response.
Consider the timing of an applicant’s request.
Separate listening from diagnosing.
lessons.keyStatement: You can recognize a request without deciding its medical or legal eligibility.

flashcards.back: A communication asking for a work-related change because of a medical condition. Special legal language is not required.
An adjustment that gives a qualified applicant with a disability an equal opportunity to compete in the selection process.
A response confirming that the request was heard and explaining the next step, without prematurely approving or denying it.
Forwarding the request to the appropriate decision maker and telling the person who that is, rather than leaving them to navigate the process alone.

items.title: When the person names a medical connection
items.body: Thank the person for describing the work barrier and explain that you will follow the agency process. Name the appropriate next contact once confirmed. A supervisor can discuss the task and requested change without asking for a diagnosis or treatment history. This keeps a useful conversation open while leaving medical documentation and eligibility questions with the responsible process.

items.title: When the next event is soon
items.body: Tell the appropriate decision maker about the upcoming interview, meeting or task. Timing can affect which authorized interim steps are useful, so a short lead time calls for prompt coordination rather than automatic rejection. Do not promise a particular adjustment or approval outside your authority. Explain the next contact to the person so they are not left to guess whether the event can be addressed.

items.title: When the need is unclear
items.body: Clarify the task that is difficult and the change the person wants considered, without converting that discussion into a medical inquiry. If the connection or next step is uncertain, consult the agency ADA Coordinator. Appearance cannot determine whether a need is genuine, and uncertainty is a reason to use the proper process rather than to dismiss the request.

tabs.heading: Requests can arrive in different ways

tabs.label: A conversation
tabs.body: A spoken request can begin the process before a form exists. For example, an employee who links a difficult workstation setup to a medical condition has given information that calls for a response. Follow the agency approach for documenting and promptly forwarding the request, and identify the decision maker to the employee. Requiring a second conversation with special terminology can leave the first request unanswered; recording the request does not authorize asking for a diagnosis.

tabs.label: An email
tabs.body: An email can identify both the requested change and an upcoming event, making timely coordination possible. Forward the request through the appropriate confidential process rather than copying the team for convenience. If the message includes medical material, seek the responsible guidance on its handling. The supervisor can clarify the work task and timing without using an email thread to gather additional medical information.

tabs.label: An application
tabs.body: An applicant’s request may concern access to an interview or test rather than how they would perform the job. Coordinate promptly with the appropriate agency contact and keep the selection criteria focused on qualifications. A format change that permits participation is not proof of lesser capability, and the applicant should not have to withdraw simply because the panel has never arranged it before. The actual accommodation decision still follows the agency process.

check.question: An employee says a medical condition makes the new work setup difficult and asks for a change. They have not filled out a form. What should the supervisor do?
check.correct: Acknowledge the request and promptly follow the agency process, telling the employee who will respond.
wrong: Ignore the request until the exact phrase reasonable accommodation appears.
Ask for the employee’s complete medical records before taking any step.
Reject the request because the employee looks well.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Ordinary communication can initiate the process. Prompt routing and a clear next step matter; eligibility and documentation belong with the responsible decision maker.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The first response should not depend on formal vocabulary, a visible disability or a supervisor’s medical inquiry. Treat the request seriously and use the appropriate process.

items.text: Because of a medical condition, I need a change in how I complete this task.
Which report template should I use?
They look healthy, so they cannot need an accommodation.
I need a disability-related adjustment for the interview.
What is the meeting agenda?
They did not say ADA, so there is no request.

lessons.next: The next lesson examines the work task without turning the conversation into a medical interview.

scenario.context: A practice applicant emails two days before an interview to request a disability-related change in the interview format. The hiring supervisor has never handled this request before.
scenario.prompt: What is the most useful first response?
options: Ask for diagnosis details and circulate them to the interview panel.
Acknowledge the request, promptly involve the appropriate agency contact and explain the next step to the applicant.
Tell the applicant to withdraw and apply next time.
responses: This seeks and spreads medical information rather than arranging an appropriate access response. Keep the selection process focused on qualifications.
This recognizes the request and its timing while involving the staff who can determine and arrange the adjustment.
This denies an equal opportunity to participate without considering the request. The short timeline makes prompt coordination important.

lessons.transfer: Write a first response to the practice analyst’s request. Include acknowledgment, the next contact and what you will confirm. Leave out a request for medical records.

move.control: You can respond promptly and make the route understandable.
move.failure: The person is asked to repeat the request until they use formal language.
move.next: Verify the agency accommodation contact and rehearse a respectful first response.

lessons.title: Discuss the work, not the diagnosis
lessons.summary: A supervisor can explain tasks and barriers while leaving medical documentation to the agency ADA Coordinator.
lessons.objective: Describe an essential function separately from one customary way of doing it.
objectives: Describe an essential function separately from one customary way of doing it.
Ask a task-focused question that does not request medical information.
Identify when a formal medical or safety question needs the responsible office.
takeaways: Focus on the task, the barrier and what an effective adjustment needs to accomplish.
A customary method is not automatically an essential function.
Supervisors must not request medical information or documentation for the accommodation process.
lessons.statement: A clear description of the work helps the process. A supervisor’s attempt to investigate the diagnosis does not.

image.caption: Work requirements can be discussed concretely without making the person disclose private medical details.

intro.heading: Describe the result and the barrier
intro.body:
An essential function is a fundamental job duty, not every habit or preference associated with the position. Reviewing a case accurately may be essential; using one particular mouse or attending every meeting from one chair may not be. The distinction requires evidence about the position and consultation when needed. A supervisor contributes knowledge of the work, but should not rewrite the job’s requirements simply to justify a preferred method or to avoid considering a request.

In a practice example, an analyst asks for a different way to review a large table because of a medical condition. The supervisor can explain the accuracy requirements, deadlines and tools involved. Useful questions include which part of the task is difficult and what the requested change would allow the person to do. Those questions keep the conversation focused on work. Asking for treatment details, a complete history or a diagnosis is a different kind of inquiry. MMB Policy 1433 directs supervisors and managers not to request medical information or documentation from a person seeking accommodation.

The ADA Coordinator can determine whether appropriate documentation is needed when the disability or need is not obvious or already known. The process should be limited to information relevant to the request, rather than broad medical records. If the employee volunteers medical information, treat it as confidential and seek the proper handling instructions. Do not place it in team notes or this course’s reflection.

Safety concerns also need evidence and the appropriate process. A diagnosis or a colleague’s discomfort is not a direct-threat determination. Bring concrete work observations to the responsible office without making a medical judgment. This allows the supervisor to contribute useful facts while protecting the person’s dignity and privacy.

inThisLesson: Separate a duty from a customary method.
Frame task-focused questions.
Recognize the medical documentation boundary.
Use evidence rather than disability assumptions.
lessons.keyStatement: Explain what the job needs to accomplish; do not assume there is only one way to accomplish it.

flashcards.back: A fundamental duty of a position, assessed using relevant evidence about the actual job. It is not automatically the usual method of performing it.
The part of a task or work environment that makes participation difficult. Describe the observable task rather than assigning a diagnosis.
A question about the activity, obstacle or effect of a possible adjustment, such as what information must be available to complete the review.
Information about disability and accommodation need requested through the authorized process. MMB Policy 1433 assigns appropriate requests to the agency ADA Coordinator.

items.title: The work result
items.body: Explain the actual function, quality requirement and timing, including why a result matters. For example, distinguish accurate table comparison from a customary screen layout. The coordinator and employee need this context to examine options. Seek guidance if you are unsure what is essential; a supervisor’s initial description should not silently redefine the job or turn a habitual method into an unchangeable requirement.

items.title: The operating conditions
items.body: Describe the tool, environment and sequence in which the employee carries out the task. An adjustment useful in a demonstration may encounter a different barrier in the real workflow. These work facts support comparison without supplying medical conclusions. Coordinate with the responsible staff and employee to examine effectiveness rather than assuming that owning a product means the task is accessible.

items.title: Observed difficulties
items.body: State the observed work event and relevant expectation without inferring a diagnosis, ability or motive. An incomplete step can have several explanations and does not justify a medical guess. For a safety or medical question, use the responsible office and case-specific process. A fear or stereotype is not a substitute for the appropriate evidence and assessment.

tabs.label: Useful work question
tabs.body: A task question identifies what the adjustment must allow the employee to do. For example, ask which table-review step is difficult and what information the employee needs to compare accurately. This can reveal a format or workflow issue without inviting a medical history. Bring the actual task requirements to the coordinator; do not assume that an employee’s useful explanation of a barrier gives permission to probe diagnosis or treatment.

tabs.label: Medical question to route
tabs.body: Medical-information and documentation questions for accommodation belong with the agency ADA Coordinator. Under Policy 1433, supervisors and managers must not request that information. A wish to help does not change that boundary. If an employee volunteers medical material, seek the appropriate confidential handling guidance rather than circulating it or adding follow-up medical questions. Keep your own contribution focused on work facts the process needs.

tabs.label: Evidence to revisit
tabs.body: A customary method may be familiar without being the essential function itself. If accurate comparison is the duty, one screen layout or manual sequence may be a means of achieving it. Describe what the job actually requires, using relevant work evidence, and seek guidance where the distinction is uncertain. This permits a meaningful discussion of alternatives without privately eliminating an essential duty or treating tradition as sufficient proof.

check.question: An employee requests a disability-related change in how they review tables. Which question is appropriate for the supervisor’s work discussion?
check.correct: Which part of the table-review task creates a barrier, and what result does the adjustment need to support?
wrong: What is your complete medical history?
Which medications do you take, and why?
Can you prove your diagnosis to the whole team?
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The question clarifies the work and needed result without requesting medical information. The coordinator handles appropriate documentation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Keep your contribution focused on the task. Medical history, medication and diagnosis requests are not the supervisor’s accommodation role under MMB Policy 1433.

items.text: The analyst must check that the listed amounts match the source records.
Do we need medical documentation for this request?
A person with that condition cannot lead a meeting.
The current tool requires repeated mouse movement to reach the fields.
What medical evidence is appropriate for a safety concern?
Our usual way of using the tool must be an essential function.

lessons.next: The next lesson follows the request to the right decision maker while protecting its confidentiality.

scenario.context: In this example, a supervisor wants to help but asks an employee to email a complete medical file before discussing a requested adjustment. The employee asks whether that is necessary.
options: Withdraw the request for medical records, focus on the work barrier and involve the ADA Coordinator about any appropriate documentation.
Insist on the file because the supervisor knows the job best.
Ask the team to vote on whether the disability seems genuine.
responses: This respects the policy’s documentation boundary and keeps useful work information available. Any volunteered medical information still needs proper confidential handling.
Knowing the job does not give the supervisor authority to request accommodation medical information.
The team does not determine disability eligibility. This exposes private information and substitutes assumptions for the process.

lessons.transfer: Choose a practice job duty. Write the result that must be achieved, one customary method and a task-focused question about an alternative.

move.control: You can provide accurate work information and avoid unnecessary medical questions.
move.failure: A familiar method is treated as essential without examining the duty.
move.next: Describe the actual task and ask the coordinator for guidance about any uncertain boundary.

lessons.title: Route the request and protect confidentiality
lessons.summary: A clear handoff includes a responsible contact and a response to the employee, with information shared only through the proper process.
lessons.objective: Identify what a prompt handoff should tell the requester.
objectives: Identify what a prompt handoff should tell the requester.
Distinguish implementation information from confidential medical and accommodation information.
Respond to a coworker’s question without disclosing another person’s accommodation.
takeaways: Tell the person who will respond; do not let forwarding become silence.
Medical information is maintained separately through the authorized process.
Even the fact of a disability-related accommodation is confidential under the state policy.
lessons.statement: Privacy is part of a workable accommodation process. People should not have to trade confidentiality for a clear response.

image.caption: A careful handoff shares the information needed for action without making it a team story.

intro.heading: Make the handoff specific and limited
intro.body:
MMB Policy 1433 directs the person receiving a request to forward it promptly to the appropriate decision maker and tell the requester who that is. The agency ADA Coordinator handles requests outside a supervisor’s or manager’s delegated authority and supports the process with the relevant staff. Agencies may delegate some decisions, but this course does not assume a particular DHS delegation or purchase limit. Verify the current agency procedure rather than treating a policy example as a local rule.

A useful handoff identifies the requested work change, timing and appropriate contact. Use the authorized communication route and avoid circulating medical details. The supervisor needs enough information to implement work restrictions and approved adjustments, not unrestricted access to the employee’s medical history. Medical documentation obtained in the process is kept separately and with limited access as the policy describes.

Confidentiality also covers the fact that a person is receiving a disability-related accommodation. If a coworker asks why someone has a different arrangement, explain the work expectations or assignment that the coworker needs to know. Do not confirm the diagnosis or accommodation status. You can say that individual personnel matters are private and that you work with each person through the appropriate process. Avoid giving details indirectly through jokes, public schedule labels or team meeting notes.

When medical information is sent to you unexpectedly, seek guidance on secure handling rather than copying it into an ordinary personnel file or shared project folder. This program’s learning notes are not an accommodation record. Keep reflections practice or non-identifying. The employee deserves an understandable route, and the people implementing a change deserve clear work instructions; both can be provided without broad disclosure.

inThisLesson: Make the handoff clear to the requester.
Verify decision authority rather than assuming it.
Limit information to authorized purposes.
Answer team questions without revealing accommodation status.
lessons.keyStatement: People can know the work arrangement they need to follow without knowing someone else’s medical situation.

flashcards.back: The responsibility assigned through the agency procedure to approve or deny a particular request. A supervisor should verify the limits of their delegation.
Access to limited information for an authorized purpose, such as implementing work restrictions. Curiosity or team interest is not enough.
Medical information and the fact of a disability-related accommodation, protected under the policy and shared only through the permitted process.
The practical direction needed to make an approved adjustment work, such as a schedule or meeting arrangement, without unnecessary medical detail.

items.title: Inform the person
items.body: Explain who has received the request and what contact you will confirm next. If the date is uncertain, say what step is pending instead of promising an outcome. This makes a handoff usable for the person while retaining the decision maker’s role. A forwarded message alone may leave the applicant or employee unsure whether anyone will respond.

items.title: Protect the information
items.body: Use the authorized confidential process for medical material and accommodation information. The coordinator handles appropriate documentation and its separate records. A supervisor may need implementation information, but that does not justify copying a medical attachment to everyone affected by a schedule. Seek the proper privacy guidance if information has already been shared rather than concealing the problem or spreading more detail.

items.title: Stay involved in the work
items.body: Forwarding a request does not end the supervisor’s implementation contribution. The coordinator may handle the decision while the supervisor arranges an approved schedule, tool or assignment. Confirm the actual responsibilities and check that the arrangement is working for its purpose. This keeps the person from having to coordinate disconnected offices alone without giving the supervisor authority over questions outside their role.

tabs.label: Employee or applicant
tabs.body: The employee or applicant needs an understandable contact and next step so they know that the request has reached the proper process. Explain who will respond and what you will confirm, without promising an unverified outcome or date. For example, forwarding an email can be followed by a clear acknowledgment. Silent forwarding may leave the person unable to distinguish active review from an unanswered request.

tabs.label: Supervisor
tabs.body: A supervisor may need restrictions and adjustment details necessary to implement the arrangement, within Policy 1433’s confidentiality limits. That is different from needing the employee’s medical history. For a schedule change, clarify the approved routine and coordination responsibilities through the proper process. Keep access limited to what implementation requires; a supervisor’s responsibility for the work is not general permission to collect or share medical details.

tabs.label: Coworker
tabs.body: A coworker may need to know who covers a meeting or when a handoff occurs. They do not ordinarily need confirmation that the arrangement is a disability accommodation. Discuss the necessary assignments and expectations without giving that confirmation or a medical reason. This allows the team to coordinate while preserving confidentiality; interest in whether an arrangement is fair is not a need-to-know decision.

check.question: A coworker asks whether an employee’s changed schedule is a disability accommodation. Which response protects confidentiality?
check.correct: Explain any work coordination the coworker needs and keep individual personnel and accommodation matters private.
wrong: Confirm the accommodation but omit the diagnosis.
Share the medical reason because the team is affected by the schedule.
Post all accommodation arrangements in the shared calendar.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Work coordination can be clear without disclosing another person’s accommodation status or medical information.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Confidentiality protects accommodation status as well as diagnosis. Confirming the status while withholding the diagnosis still discloses protected information. A schedule effect does not justify sharing a medical reason. A shared calendar should convey necessary work coordination, not publish everyone’s accommodation arrangements. Explain the assignments the coworker needs and use the appropriate confidential process for individual matters.

items.text: The medical documentation requested appropriately by the ADA Coordinator.
The meeting time that participants need to attend.
A team note naming a colleague’s diagnosis and accommodation.
The coordinator’s formal record of the approved adjustment.
Who covers the afternoon task under the agreed work schedule.
An email to the entire unit confirming why a colleague receives accommodation.

lessons.next: The next lesson compares effective work adjustments without making a unilateral formal decision.

scenario.context: In this example, a supervisor receives a request by email and forwards the entire medical attachment to the team so colleagues understand the proposed work change.
options: Leave the email in place because good intentions make the disclosure acceptable.
Explain even more medical detail so nobody misunderstands.
Seek the appropriate privacy and ADA guidance promptly, stop further circulation and coordinate work with only the necessary information.
responses: Good intentions do not remove confidentiality obligations. An inappropriate disclosure needs the responsible response.
More disclosure increases the problem. Work coordination does not require a medical explanation to the team.
This addresses the disclosure through the proper offices and limits future sharing. Follow their directions rather than inventing a remedy or concealing what happened.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice handoff note naming the work barrier, requested adjustment and timing. Then remove anything the receiving work coordinator does not need.

move.control: You can use a clear, limited handoff and protect the person’s privacy.
move.failure: An entire email thread or medical attachment is shared for convenience.
move.next: Verify the authorized request route and what implementation information your role may receive.

lessons.title: Help compare effective adjustments
lessons.summary: Contribute knowledge of the job while the authorized process considers the person’s needs, effective options and relevant limits.
lessons.objective: Compare two possible adjustments by their effect on an essential task.
objectives: Compare two possible adjustments by their effect on an essential task.
Explain why the employee’s preference matters without promising it is always the only option.
Route concerns about undue hardship or direct threat for case-specific review.
takeaways: An accommodation must be effective for the purpose it serves.
The person’s preference deserves serious consideration; another effective option may be considered.
Do not decide from stereotypes, coworker preference or the team’s small budget alone.
lessons.statement: Comparing options is a shared inquiry into what works. It is not a contest over who deserves an adjustment.

image.caption: A work discussion can compare options while respecting the employee’s experience and decision authority.

intro.heading: Compare the effect, not just the price
intro.body:
A practice analyst requests one software tool to address a disability-related work barrier. The team already owns a different tool. The supervisor can describe the tasks and arrange a useful discussion through the accommodation process, but cannot assume the existing tool is effective merely because it is available. The employee’s experience of the barrier is important evidence about whether an option allows the required work.

MMB Policy 1433 says the employee’s preference is seriously considered, while an effective alternative may be offered. This does not make cost the only question or allow any cheaper option to count as sufficient. Ask what the adjustment needs to accomplish: accurate review, equal participation in required training or access to an employment benefit. Compare options against that purpose, including how they work in the actual environment. The appropriate decision maker determines the accommodation with the necessary consultation.

A supervisor contributes the essential duties, operating conditions and implementation facts. A request does not automatically require removing an essential function or lowering a uniformly applied production standard. It may involve a different method, tool, schedule or other effective adjustment. If no effective adjustment appears available, seek the coordinator’s guidance about the full process, including reassignment considerations when applicable; do not improvise a dismissal.

Concerns about undue hardship or direct threat need the required case-specific assessment. A diagnosis, fear, coworker irritation or local budget shortage is not enough. MMB requires ADA Coordinator involvement before denial, and financial-resource denial requires additional consultation under the policy. A direct-threat question depends on individualized, objective evidence about a significant risk, not a general belief about disability. Your role is to surface useful facts and carry out authorized decisions.

inThisLesson: Define what an effective option must accomplish.
Consider the employee’s preference seriously.
Separate duties from methods.
Route formal limits for proper assessment.
lessons.keyStatement: A less expensive option is useful only if it is effective for the person’s work need.

flashcards.back: An adjustment that addresses the relevant barrier and provides the employment opportunity it is intended to support.
The adjustment the person wants considered. The policy calls for serious consideration while allowing another effective option.
Significant difficulty or expense assessed case by case with relevant agency resources and operating factors through the authorized process.
A formal assessment of a significant risk of substantial harm that cannot be eliminated or reduced through reasonable accommodation; it must rely on individualized objective evidence.

items.title: State the purpose
items.body: State what the adjustment must enable in the actual work activity. Without that purpose, a cheaper product and a requested product may look interchangeable simply because their names are similar. Describe the required result and relevant environment so the comparison can examine effectiveness. Do not decide that familiarity with an option proves it meets the employee’s need.

items.title: Ask about the options
items.body: Consider each option for the employee, task and environment, seriously considering the employee’s preference. Ask how a proposed option would remove the barrier, and use appropriate specialist input through the process when needed. A coworker’s convenience or a general product demonstration does not establish effectiveness. The agency may consider another effective option, but should not substitute an untested assumption for a case-specific comparison.

items.title: Use the correct decision route
items.body: Provide relevant implementation facts through the authorized process and confirm actual agency decision authority. The ADA Coordinator guides questions concerning documentation, hardship, direct threat and denial. A low local budget does not by itself settle the agency-wide resource question. Before denying a request, use the required consultation rather than turning a supervisor’s work comparison into a unilateral final determination.

tabs.label: The job duty
tabs.body: The job duty describes the result the position must accomplish, supported by actual work evidence. Accurate review may be essential even when a particular tool is not. An overly narrow description can make a useful alternative appear impossible; an overly broad one can conceal a real requirement. Contribute clear task facts and seek appropriate guidance rather than redefining the position privately to approve or deny a request.

tabs.label: The method
tabs.body: The method describes how a duty is performed. A different format or tool may preserve the essential result while removing a barrier, but that possibility needs examination for this employee and task. A product demonstration alone does not establish effectiveness in the actual environment. Explain the workflow and consider the employee’s experience through the accommodation process, without making coworker preference the deciding criterion.

tabs.label: The formal decision
tabs.body: The formal decision determines whether and which accommodation will be provided, or explains a denial through the applicable procedure. A supervisor’s useful work comparison is an input, not automatically the final decision. Check actual agency delegation and involve the ADA Coordinator as required. An effective alternative may be considered, with the employee’s preference seriously considered; local price or familiarity alone does not settle effectiveness or hardship.

check.question: The team owns a cheaper tool than the one an employee requested. What is the sound next step?
check.correct: Compare whether it is effective for the relevant task through the accommodation process, seriously considering the employee’s preference.
wrong: Use it automatically because lower cost proves reasonableness.
Deny the request because coworkers prefer the current tool.
Promise the requested product immediately without checking authority or effectiveness.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Availability and price do not establish effectiveness. The employee’s needs and the task must be considered through the proper decision process.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Lower cost alone does not establish effectiveness, and coworker preference cannot decide the accommodation. An immediate promise may exceed authority and skip the work comparison. Examine the relevant task, the employee’s need and preference, effective options and actual decision process. A supervisor’s contribution informs that process rather than replacing it.

items.text: The proposed tool lets the employee review every required field accurately.
Everyone else likes the current tool, so it must work for this person.
Does the proposed adjustment create undue hardship under the applicable process?
The employee explains why the current format does not address the barrier.
A diagnosis means the person is unsafe in every setting.
What evidence is needed for a direct-threat assessment?

lessons.next: The next lesson examines delay and implementation, where even an approved decision can fail in practice.

scenario.context: In this example, a supervisor proposes a tool already owned by the agency. The employee explains that it does not remove the task barrier. The supervisor wants to deny the request because the local budget is low.
options: Deny immediately and tell the employee to manage with the existing tool.
Ask coworkers whether they think the employee really needs another tool.
Bring the effectiveness and resource questions to the ADA Coordinator and follow the case-specific process.
responses: The existing tool’s availability does not establish effectiveness, and the local budget alone does not justify a unilateral denial.
Coworker opinion is not the appropriate accommodation assessment and may expose confidential information.
This puts the relevant facts before the responsible decision process. Continue communicating with the employee and consider authorized interim steps.

lessons.transfer: Compare two practice options for a task. Write what each allows the person to do, what remains uncertain and what question needs the decision maker.

move.control: You can provide task and implementation facts without making an unsupported denial.
move.failure: A familiar or inexpensive option is assumed effective without checking.
move.next: Ask how each option addresses the identified barrier and route formal limits through the coordinator.

lessons.title: Keep the person informed while work proceeds
lessons.summary: Approval, delay and implementation need communication and follow-through, not a silent handoff.
lessons.objective: Distinguish an approved adjustment from one actually implemented.
objectives: Distinguish an approved adjustment from one actually implemented.
Plan a status update and possible temporary measure during a delay.
Identify the state policy’s 30-day status requirement without treating it as a general permission to wait.
takeaways: The policy calls for prompt processing and provision in as short a timeframe as possible.
If an approved accommodation cannot be provided within a reasonable time, the policy requires a status update before the end of 30 days.
Feasible temporary assistance and clear follow-up can matter while a longer step is pending.
lessons.statement: A person needs to know what is happening and how they can work in the meantime. Approval alone does not remove a barrier.

image.caption: Follow-through connects a decision to the work arrangement the person actually experiences.

intro.heading: Make implementation visible and usable
intro.body:
In this example, an employee’s accommodation is approved, but the necessary equipment has not arrived. The supervisor assumes the matter is complete because the approval email was sent. The employee is still unable to complete part of the task. This is an implementation gap: a formal decision has not yet become an effective work arrangement. The supervisor should coordinate with the responsible staff rather than leaving the employee to chase each office alone.

MMB Policy 1433 calls for processing and providing an approved accommodation in as short a timeframe as possible. The time required can depend on the nature of the adjustment and the supporting information needed. If an approved accommodation cannot be provided within a reasonable time, the decision maker informs the requester of its status before the end of 30 days. This is a status safeguard, not permission to delay every request for 30 days or a promise that every request is resolved in that period. Where feasible during delay, temporary measures provide assistance.

A useful update explains the pending step, the responsible contact, what is currently available and when the next update will occur. Do not invent a delivery date or say the accommodation is working before the person can use it. Ask the appropriate decision maker about temporary options; a supervisor should not substitute an unapproved arrangement that fails the need or creates another problem.

Once implemented, check that the adjustment actually addresses the work barrier. A new tool may need configuration or instruction; a meeting arrangement may fail when a facilitator forgets it. Confirm the agreed routine and respond when circumstances change. Keep the necessary accommodation record through the authorized process, not in team learning notes. Follow-through is a continuing work responsibility, not a demand that the employee prove gratitude for assistance.

inThisLesson: Identify an implementation gap.
Communicate a delay clearly.
Consider feasible temporary support through the process.
Verify that the adjustment works.
lessons.keyStatement: Report the request’s actual status: pending, approved, implemented or needing further attention.

flashcards.back: A difference between an approved adjustment and what is available in the person’s actual work.
A clear explanation of what has happened, what remains, who is responsible and when the person will next hear from the process.
Feasible assistance while a longer accommodation step is pending, considered through the appropriate process.
A follow-up about whether the adjustment addresses the barrier in actual work, without reopening medical questions unnecessarily.

items.title: The current step
items.body: Explain whether the request is still under consideration, approved or awaiting implementation. These are different states with different next steps. An approval does not remove a barrier while equipment is delayed. Share a confirmed status and the responsible next action; do not invent a delivery date to make the update sound more reassuring.

items.title: The immediate work arrangement
items.body: Coordinate with responsible staff about feasible temporary assistance during a delay, then examine whether it helps with the task. A temporary arrangement is not automatically the final accommodation or permission to stop pursuing an approved change. Keep its purpose and limits clear, protect confidentiality and continue communication while the longer step remains pending.

items.title: The next contact
items.body: Identify the responsible contact and a realistic next update. Policy 1433 calls for prompt processing and includes a conditional status update before the end of 30 days when an approved accommodation cannot be provided within a reasonable time. That is not permission to wait silently or a universal completion guarantee. Continue appropriate communication even when another office owns the pending step.

tabs.heading: Check the arrangement, not just the email

tabs.label: Equipment or software
tabs.body: A purchase order shows a procurement step; it does not show that equipment is delivered, configured or usable for the approved purpose. Coordinate with responsible staff to check the actual task and address a remaining barrier. For example, a tool may arrive but still need configuration. Keep the person informed and pursue appropriate temporary assistance during a delay rather than treating approval or ordering as completion.

tabs.label: Schedule or location
tabs.body: A schedule or location adjustment needs an understood routine and necessary work coordination. Confirm the approved arrangement with the responsible staff and employee, then communicate only the assignment information others need. A shared calendar can show availability without announcing accommodation status. If the routine is not working, return to the proper process rather than assuming the original approval answers every new practical question.

tabs.label: Meetings and training
tabs.body: Recurring support should be arranged for the occasions covered by the approved accommodation. Policy 1433 distinguishes regular recurring arrangements from repeated needs that may require appropriate advance notice, rather than a new written request each time. Confirm which arrangement applies and who coordinates it. A support booking for one training session does not by itself establish that the next relevant session is covered.

check.question: What does the state policy’s 30-day language mean for an approved accommodation that cannot be provided within a reasonable time?
check.correct: The decision maker gives a status update before the end of 30 days; the policy still calls for prompt provision and feasible temporary assistance.
wrong: Every request may be ignored for 30 days.
Every request is guaranteed to be completed exactly on day 30.
No communication is needed until equipment arrives.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The provision is a status safeguard in the circumstances described, not a general waiting period or universal completion deadline.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The 30-day provision is not a permission to ignore a request, an exact completion guarantee for every request or a reason to remain silent until delivery. It requires a status update in the circumstances described for an approved accommodation delayed beyond a reasonable time. Prompt provision, continued communication and feasible temporary assistance remain important.

items.text: The approved tool is installed and the employee confirms it supports the task.
The adjustment is approved, but the equipment is still on order.
The tool arrived but still cannot access the required fields.
The agreed recurring meeting support is in place and its usefulness was confirmed.
The schedule adjustment is approved, but coordination has not been completed.
A software update has stopped an earlier adjustment from working.

lessons.next: The final lesson connects accommodation, work expectations and respectful follow-up without turning disability into a performance assumption.

scenario.context: In this example, an employee’s equipment is approved but delayed. They ask for an update and explain that the barrier is still affecting the task.
scenario.prompt: What is the supervisor’s best contribution?
options: Tell the employee approval means the problem is solved.
Coordinate a clear status update and feasible temporary support with the responsible staff, then verify implementation.
Tell the team the employee’s medical history to explain the delay.
responses: Approval is not implementation. The employee’s current work barrier still needs a response.
This provides a useful response without promising an unsupported date or replacing the formal process. Continue until the adjustment is implemented and checked.
Medical disclosure is unnecessary for arranging work and would undermine confidentiality.

lessons.transfer: Draft a status update for a practice delayed adjustment: current step, responsible contact, possible interim support and next update. Do not invent a delivery date.

move.control: You can coordinate implementation and keep communication clear.
move.failure: An approval or forwarded request is treated as the end of the supervisor’s role.
move.next: Confirm what is actually available and ask the responsible process about delay and interim support.

lessons.title: Maintain fair expectations and revisit what works
lessons.summary: Clear work expectations and effective accommodation can operate together, with appropriate support when a barrier changes.
lessons.objective: Separate observed work facts from disability-based assumptions in a performance discussion.
objectives: Separate observed work facts from disability-based assumptions in a performance discussion.
Respond to a new accommodation request even when a performance concern also exists.
Identify when an approved arrangement needs follow-up because the task or circumstances changed.
takeaways: Describe work performance with relevant facts and consistent expectations.
A performance concern does not remove the duty to consider a new accommodation request.
A changed task or ineffective adjustment deserves a new conversation through the proper process.
lessons.statement: Fairness means examining the work and the access conditions clearly, rather than assuming disability explains either success or difficulty.

image.caption: Useful feedback is specific about the work and open to a needed adjustment.

intro.heading: Keep the discussion evidence-based
intro.body:
A supervisor can maintain clear, job-related work expectations while supporting an accommodation process. The ADA does not automatically require removing essential functions or lowering uniformly applied production standards. It can require effective adjustments that let a qualified employee meet those expectations or access employment benefits. A different method or schedule should not be treated as lower ability merely because it differs from the team’s usual practice.

When a performance concern arises, describe the actual work: what was expected, what happened, when it happened and what relevant support was available. Do not use a diagnosis as an explanation for a mistake or assume a person with a disability cannot take on development opportunities. Consult HR and the ADA Coordinator where performance, conduct and accommodation questions overlap. This course does not decide discipline, legal eligibility or a particular employee’s outcome.

In a practice case, an analyst receives feedback about an incomplete report and then requests a disability-related adjustment to a tool. A request does not necessarily erase prior performance issues, but it still needs a timely prospective response through the accommodation process. The supervisor should not reject it as too late simply because feedback has already occurred. The relevant offices can help separate the questions and consider the facts.

Continue checking an approved adjustment when the work changes. A new system, location or meeting format may reintroduce a barrier. Ask about effectiveness and promptly route a needed change; do not demand repeated medical proof on your own. Accommodation is not a one-time favor or a reason to limit a person’s career. The supervisor’s lasting contribution is clear work, protected privacy and reliable follow-through.

inThisLesson: Describe performance with specific work facts.
Consider a request without erasing separate questions.
Avoid limiting opportunity based on disability.
Revisit an arrangement when the task changes.
lessons.keyStatement: Be specific about the work, and remain responsive to the access conditions in which it is done.

flashcards.back: A relevant work or production requirement applied fairly, with the necessary accommodation process considered.
An adjustment considered for work going forward. A new request still requires response when earlier performance concerns exist.
Facts about actual work and applicable expectations rather than a diagnosis, stereotype or inference about motivation.
A new task, tool or condition that may affect whether an earlier adjustment remains effective.

items.title: What happened in the work?
items.body: Describe the relevant work facts and expectations with appropriate HR guidance where needed. An incomplete report does not prove a disability-based cause or motive. Consistent supervision and accommodation responsibilities can both matter. Keep the factual performance discussion separate from medical assumptions and from a premature conclusion about a new requested adjustment.

items.title: What access need is being raised?
items.body: Recognize and route a newly raised accommodation request promptly even if a performance question is unresolved. The process can consider prospective needs without automatically erasing earlier facts or determining every performance outcome. HR and the ADA Coordinator can guide the overlapping questions. The team does not decide the request through opinions about fairness or the employee’s disability.

items.title: What needs revisiting?
items.body: A changed task or an adjustment that no longer works calls for renewed communication through the responsible process. Identify what has changed in the actual work, and examine current effectiveness with the employee and appropriate staff. Do not use the old approval as proof that a new barrier is solved. Equally, do not promise a replacement without the necessary assessment and authority.

tabs.label: Daily supervision
tabs.body: Daily supervision uses specific work facts, usable instructions and relevant expectations. Describe an incomplete report without assuming that disability explains it or asking medical questions. If the employee raises an accommodation need, respond through that process as well. Separating the questions prevents both automatic rejection of a request and an unsupported conclusion that the request settles every earlier performance issue.

tabs.label: Learning and development
tabs.body: Accommodation can concern equal access to employment benefits and privileges, including training. Discuss the actual opportunity and requested support through the proper process rather than excluding an employee because arrangements may take effort. A development invitation and an effective participation arrangement are separate steps. Consider what the person needs to participate without publicly disclosing their accommodation or predicting their ability from disability.

tabs.label: Changes in the workplace
tabs.body: A new system or schedule may alter the task for which an adjustment worked. Coordinate early where possible, recognize a new request and examine current effectiveness with the responsible staff. Prior success is useful context, not a guarantee that every update preserves access. Keep ordinary work coordination and confidential accommodation decisions distinct, so the employee is neither left with an obsolete arrangement nor promised an unexamined replacement.

check.question: An employee requests an accommodation after receiving performance feedback. Which response is sound?
check.correct: Respond to the request prospectively through the accommodation process while handling any separate performance question with appropriate guidance.
wrong: Reject the request automatically because feedback came first.
Assume the request erases every earlier performance fact.
Share the request with coworkers and ask whether it is fair.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The questions may overlap but need careful separation. The request requires a response; HR and the ADA Coordinator can guide the relevant decisions.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Feedback coming first does not automatically eliminate a prospective accommodation request. The request also does not by itself erase every earlier performance fact or decide the outcome. Sharing it with coworkers and asking them to judge fairness would compromise confidentiality and substitute a team vote for the responsible process. Address both questions through their proper roles and guidance.

sorting.heading: Use evidence and the correct route

items.text: The required field was missing from the report submitted on the stated date.
Their diagnosis means they cannot supervise others.
Route the new disability-related adjustment request promptly.
The software update removed the keyboard access used in the approved arrangement.
Receiving accommodation means the person should not get development opportunities.
Ask HR and the ADA Coordinator to guide overlapping performance and accommodation questions.

lessons.next: Use the job aid for a clear first response and follow-through. Continue with the interactive-process course for deeper practice in a shared accommodation conversation.

scenario.context: In this example, an employee’s earlier accommodation worked well. A new software version creates a barrier, and their supervisor notices an incomplete report. The employee requests a change.
options: Treat the incomplete report as proof that the employee’s disability makes them unsuitable.
Ignore the report and promise any requested tool without the process.
Describe the work facts, promptly route the change request and coordinate with HR and the ADA Coordinator where needed.
responses: This substitutes a disability-based inference for work evidence and ignores the changed access conditions.
The work and accommodation questions both need attention through their proper routes; an unsupported promise does not resolve them.
This keeps expectations clear and responds to the new barrier without making a medical judgment or deciding the outcome prematurely.

lessons.transfer: Write two separate practice notes: one describing a work fact and one describing the next accommodation step. Remove diagnosis assumptions and personal identifying information.

move.control: You can maintain clear expectations and remain responsive to changed barriers.
move.failure: A disability label replaces work evidence or becomes a reason to limit opportunity.
move.next: Review a practice changed-task case with the job aid and identify the appropriate contacts.

jobAid.subtitle: A supervisor’s response and follow-through
remember: Special legal words and a visible disability are not required for a request.
Discuss the task; do not request accommodation medical information or records.
Follow verified agency decision authority. Contact the ADA Coordinator before denial.
Accommodation status and medical information are confidential. Use practice examples in learning notes.

sections.heading: Receive and route
items: Acknowledge the request in plain language.
Promptly forward it through the authorized route and tell the requester who will respond.
Explain any next step without promising an outcome outside your authority.

sections.heading: Contribute and implement
items: Describe essential duties, actual work conditions and the barrier.
Compare options by effectiveness, seriously considering the person’s preference through the process.
Coordinate the approved adjustment and any feasible temporary measures during delay.

sections.heading: Check and maintain
items: Distinguish approval from implementation and verify effectiveness.
Keep the person informed and follow the policy’s status requirements in the circumstances they describe.
Revisit changed tasks, protect privacy and seek appropriate guidance when work and accommodation questions overlap.
